title: Can, could, be able to and be allowed to
subtitle: I can / was able to / was allowed to
summary: Choose between can, could, be able to and be allowed to when you talk about ability, possibility and permission.

lesson.heading: When we avoid be able to
lesson.text: We sometimes use be able to instead of can and could for ability, but we avoid it when we talk about something happening as we speak, before a passive, and when the meaning is 'know how to'.

examples.text: Watch me, Mum; **I can** stand on one leg.
examples.wrong: I'm able to stand on one leg

examples.note: rather than Films are now easily able to be streamed ...
= do you know how to; rather than Are you able to cook?

lesson.heading: General ability or one particular achievement?

left.label: A general ability - could
examples: Sophie **could** play the flute quite well. (or ... **was able to** ...)

right.label: A single achievement - was / were able to
examples: She swam strongly and **was able to** cross the river easily, even though it was swollen by the heavy rain. (not She swam strongly and could cross ...)

lesson.heading: When could is more natural
lesson.text: Could is usually more natural than be able to in negative sentences; with verbs of the senses (feel, hear, see, smell, taste) and of thinking (believe, decide, remember, understand); after the only thing / place / time and after all meaning 'the only thing'; and with almost, hardly, just and nearly.

examples.text: I tried to get up but **I couldn't** move.
**I could** remember the crash, but nothing after that.
All we **could** see were his feet.

left.label: could - theoretically possible
examples: It **could** be expensive to keep a cat. (= if we had one, it could or it may not be expensive)

right.label: can - possible and it really happens
examples: It **can** be expensive to keep a cat. (= it can be, and it sometimes is)

lesson.heading: can't for impossibility
lesson.text: We use can't, not couldn't, to say that something is theoretically or actually impossible.

examples.text: There **can't** be many people in the world who haven't watched television.
The doctor **can't** see you this morning; he's busy at the hospital.

lesson.heading: A real possibility, or some doubt?

left.label: can - a very real possibility
examples: We **can** stay with Jake in Oslo. (= we will be able to stay)

right.label: could - less likely, some doubt
examples: We **could** stay with Jake in Oslo. (= it's possible; if he's there)

lesson.heading: Permission: could and be allowed to
lesson.text: For general permission in the past - permission to do something at any time - we can use either could or was / were allowed to. For permission for one particular past action we use was / were allowed to, not could. In negative sentences either form works.

examples.text: Anyone **was allowed to** fish in the lake when the council owned it.
Although he didn't have a ticket, Ned **was allowed to** come in.
I **couldn't / wasn't allowed to** open the present until my birthday.

exercises.prompt: Look at me, I ___ ride my bike without any help!
exercises.explanation: For something happening as we speak we use can, not be able to.

exercises.prompt: Valuables ___ in the hotel safe. Please ask at the reception desk.
exercises.explanation: Before a passive we use can, not be able to.

exercises.prompt: We ___ finish the hockey match before it started snowing too heavily.
exercises.explanation: One particular past achievement takes was / were able to, not could.

exercises.prompt: I knew Petra had been decorating. I ___ smell the paint when I came in.
exercises.explanation: With verbs of the senses such as smell, could is more natural.

exercises.prompt: The air was so polluted in the city centre, I ___ breathe.
exercises.explanation: With hardly (and almost, just, nearly) could is more natural.

exercises.prompt: She looked all over the house, but ___ find her keys anywhere.
exercises.explanation: In negative sentences couldn't is more natural than wasn't able to.

exercises.prompt: Which form fits each gap better - could(n't) or was / were able to?

items.text: I tried to get up but I ___ move.
We ___ finish the hockey match before it started snowing too heavily.
All we ___ see were his feet.
When the firefighters arrived they ___ put out the flames in a couple of minutes.
I was very busy at work, but I ___ have a couple of days off last week.

exercises.prompt: We went camping in the north of Spain last July. As you probably know, it ___ rain a lot on the coast, even in midsummer.
exercises.explanation: It really does rain there, so can, not could - could would make it only theoretical.

exercises.prompt: Now, there ___ be many people who haven't had difficulty putting up a tent at some time, but it took us more than two hours.
exercises.explanation: For something that is (almost) impossible we use can't, not couldn't.

exercises.statement: Although he didn't have a ticket, Ned could come in.
exercises.explanation: Although he didn't have a ticket, Ned was allowed to come in. Permission for one particular action takes was allowed to.

exercises.prompt: The hotel was full, but they were very kind and we ___ camp at the end of their garden!
exercises.explanation: Permission for one particular action, so was / were allowed to, not could.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to say who had permission to fish before the lake changed hands.
exercises.answer: Anyone was allowed to fish in the lake when the council owned it.
exercises.explanation: This is general permission in the past, so could fish is also possible here.
